situation:
You are the financial analyst at IRONGATE SHIPWORKS, a shipbuilding and repair yard that builds barges and overhauls working vessels. The controller (judge) has asked you to recommend what the yard should do about a large stock of steel plate it inherited eight months ago when it merged with a smaller repair yard, and about an offer that arrived with it.

The two yards still keep separate inventory records, and nobody has finished reconciling them. Most of the inherited steel plate and marine fittings no longer fit anything the yard builds, and accounting standards require stock like that to be carried at what it can actually fetch rather than what was paid for it. Written down, it lands on this quarter.

A defense contractor has offered the yard a multi-year hull repair contract and has offered to buy the inherited steel plate at close to the price it is carried at, which would leave nothing to write down. It would run the yard's shop floor to the contractor's schedule and put its most experienced welders on the contractor's hulls.

Those welders are the same people who teach the apprenticeship program the yard runs with the local technical college, a program it promised publicly to keep going after the merger and the way it has recruited and trained every welder it employs. Taking the multi-year hull repair contract avoids the write-down and brings in years of work, and it costs the yard that promise, the apprentices' shop time, and a name built on training its own.

Declining the contract keeps the apprenticeship program and the promise intact, and it costs the yard the write-down on the inherited steel plate, landing on this quarter's results while the merger is still unfinished, and the largest piece of new work anyone has offered the yard in years.

The controller (judge) has asked you to explain what accounting standards say about carrying stock at that value, explain why the yard's welders need to keep learning, describe how the apprenticeship program gives newcomers work experience, explain what the yard's name is built on, and say how trust with the college would be kept either way.

The controller (judge) will greet you and ask to hear your ideas. After you have presented and answered the questions, the controller (judge) will thank you for your work.
judgeCharacterization:
You are the controller (judge) of IRONGATE SHIPWORKS. Business background is the same as the situation above.

The merger is eight months old and still unfinished, and the write-down on the inherited steel plate would land on this quarter. You want the financial analyst to explain what accounting standards say about carrying stock at that value, explain why the yard's welders need to keep learning, describe how the apprenticeship program gives newcomers work experience, explain what the yard's name is built on, say how trust with the local technical college would be kept either way, and tell you plainly whether to take the multi-year hull repair contract or decline it.

After the financial analyst has presented, you will ask the following questions:
judgeQuestions: What would the path we did not take have given the yard?
If we had gone the other way, what would that have cost us?
